# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to own and control their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, especially for large teams, since it can be self-hosted on the user's own servers.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Good customer support
* User-friendly interface
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Customizable and extensible
* Free to use
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple and easy-to-use communication platform. It's also a good option for teams that don't require a high level of customization or control over their data. On the other hand, Element is a good choice for large teams or organizations that require a high level of security, customization, and control over their data. It's also a good option for teams that want to self-host their communication platform and have the technical expertise to do so.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which exports data in a JSON format.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any additional settings or integrations as needed.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for teams that value security, customization, and control over their data, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching to Element if you have the technical expertise and resources to do so.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of less than 10 users who don't need a lot of integrations with third-party apps
* Teams that require end-to-end encryption for all conversations and have the technical expertise to set up and maintain an Element server
* Large teams or organizations that want to self-host their communication platform and have the resources to do so
* Teams that don't need a high level of customer support and are comfortable with troubleshooting issues themselves
* Teams that value security and customization above ease of use

## FAQ
### What is the main difference between Slack and Element?
The main difference between Slack and Element is that Element is self-hosted and open-source, while Slack is a proprietary platform.
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free to use, but you will need to self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain than Slack.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.
### Is Element more secure than Slack?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for paid plans.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular team collaboration platforms that offer a range of features for communication, file sharing, and integration with other tools. This comparison is useful for teams looking to switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those who value data ownership and self-hosting capabilities. The core use case for both tools is team communication and collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost is free for self-hosted deployments, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed for large-scale deployments, while Slack can become expensive for very large teams.
* Integration: Mattermost has a more extensive range of integrations with development tools, such as GitLab and Jira, while Slack has a broader range of integrations with other SaaS applications.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with other SaaS applications
* Good mobile apps
* Strong support for video and audio calls
* Limited control over data ownership and storage
**Mattermost:**
* Free for self-hosted deployments
* High degree of customizability and extensibility
* Strong support for development teams and integrations with development tools
* Can be more complex to set up and manage
* Limited support for video and audio calls

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams who value ease of use and a wide range of integrations with other SaaS applications. It's particularly well-suited for small to medium-sized teams who don't have the technical expertise or resources to manage a self-hosted deployment. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest in setting up and managing a self-hosted deployment. It's particularly well-suited for large teams or enterprises who need a high degree of customizability and extensibility.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a third-party tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with other tools or services.
5. Test your Mattermost deployment to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, with a wide range of features and a high degree of customizability and extensibility. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's support for video and audio calls is currently limited. For teams who rely heavily on video conferencing, Slack may still be a better choice. Overall, we recommend Mattermost for teams who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest in setting up and managing a self-hosted deployment.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need video conferencing and want to save money on per-user costs.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest in setting up and managing a self-hosted deployment.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) who need a high degree of customizability and extensibility, and are willing to invest in setting up and managing a self-hosted deployment.
* Development teams who rely heavily on integrations with development tools, such as GitLab and Jira.
* Teams who are currently using Slack's free plan and are looking for a more scalable and customizable solution.

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost is free for self-hosted deployments. You'll need to pay for server costs, but there are no per-user fees.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost can be more complex to set up and manage, particularly for self-hosted deployments. However, it offers a wide range of features and a high degree of customizability and extensibility.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with other tools and services?
Yes, Mattermost has a wide range of integrations with other tools and services, including development tools like GitLab and Jira.
### Does Mattermost support video and audio calls?
Currently, Mattermost's support for video and audio calls is limited. If you rely heavily on video conferencing, Slack may still be a better choice.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for community building and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution. The core use case for both tools is real-time messaging and voice/video conferencing, with the key reason to switch being data ownership and control.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted, with costs limited to server maintenance.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's data ownership is subject to their terms of service.
* Setup complexity: Discord has a more straightforward setup process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable due to its self-hosted nature, allowing users to add more resources as needed.
* Feature difference: Element has native integration with the Matrix protocol, allowing for seamless communication with other Matrix-compatible platforms, whereas Discord does not.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $0.005-$0.01 per user (depending on the plan) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $0.005-$0.01 per user (depending on the plan) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Discord:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and user base
* Robust features for gaming and community building
* Mobile and desktop applications
* Limitations on data ownership and control
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Full data ownership and control
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Native integration with the Matrix protocol
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams, gaming communities, and individuals who prioritize ease of use and a large user base. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for larger organizations, enterprises, and individuals who require full data ownership and control, as well as high scalability and customization.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and create a new account.
3. Import your exported data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure your Element server and settings to match your Discord setup.
5. Test and verify that all features and data are working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its self-hosting requirements and technical complexity. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's self-hosting setup can be resource-intensive, requiring significant server resources and technical expertise. However, for organizations and individuals who require full data ownership and control, Element is a clear choice, and we recommend switching from Discord to Element for those who prioritize these features.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need advanced gaming features
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who prioritize data ownership and control
* Large organizations (over 100 users) who require high scalability and customization
* Enterprises with strict data security and compliance requirements
* Individuals who value open-source software and community-driven development

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for gaming?
Element can be used for gaming, but it may not have the same level of gaming-specific features as Discord. However, Element's self-hosted nature and customization options make it a viable alternative for gaming communities.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
Element is not directly compatible with Discord, but it can integrate with other Matrix-compatible platforms, allowing for seamless communication between users on different platforms.
### Can I self-host Element on my own server?
Yes, Element can be self-hosted on your own server, giving you full control over your data and settings.
### Does Element have mobile and desktop applications?
Yes, Element has mobile and desktop applications, allowing users to access their accounts and communicate on-the-go.
### Is Element free?
Element is free and open-source, with no costs associated with using the software itself, although server costs may apply for self-hosting.

Notion and AppFlowy are two popular tools for note-taking, collaboration, and project management. Both tools cater to individuals and teams seeking to streamline their workflow and improve productivity. The core use case for both tools is to provide an all-in-one workspace for organizing tasks, notes, and projects, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or reduce costs.

* Cost: Notion charges $8-$20 per user per month, while AppFlowy is free.
* Data ownership: AppFlowy allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control over their information, whereas Notion stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Notion has a more user-friendly interface and is generally easier to set up, while AppFlowy requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: AppFlowy is designed to be highly scalable, making it suitable for large teams and enterprises, whereas Notion's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.

|--------|----------|---------|

| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |

| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1600-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons

* Wide range of templates and integrations
* Strong mobile app support
* Collaborative features

**AppFlowy:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting capabilities

It is ideal for teams that need a user-friendly interface and are willing to pay for the convenience. AppFlowy, on the other hand, is designed for larger teams or enterprises that require high scalability, customization, and control over their data. It is ideal for teams with technical expertise who want to self-host their data and have native integration with GitHub.

## Migration Path

2. Set up an AppFlowy instance on your server or use a hosted service.
3. Use the AppFlowy import tool to migrate your Notion data.

One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that AppFlowy requires a high degree of technical expertise to self-host and customize. No, Notion does not offer self-hosting options. All data is stored on Notion's proprietary servers.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control systems that help developers manage and collaborate on coding projects. This comparison is beneficial for development teams, especially those considering switching from GitHub to GitLab due to concerns about data ownership, cost, or specific feature requirements. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data ownership and costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data Ownership: GitLab allows for self-hosting, giving users full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: GitHub is generally easier to set up, especially for small projects, while GitLab requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option provides more flexibility for large enterprises.
* Feature Difference: GitLab offers built-in CI/CD pipelines, while GitHub requires third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Limited control over data ownership
**GitLab:**
* Offers self-hosting for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD pipelines
* Free self-hosted option with more features
* More complex setup process
* Limited support for some third-party integrations

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the GitHub ecosystem. GitLab, on the other hand, is ideal for larger enterprises or teams that require self-hosting for data ownership and control. It's also a good option for teams that need built-in CI/CD pipelines and are willing to invest time in setup and configuration.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the import page.
3. Use the GitHub import tool to import your repository, or upload the archive file manually.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as CI/CD pipelines and permissions.
5. Test your migrated repository to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for most users, offering a robust set of features and self-hosting capabilities. However, one technical limitation to consider is GitLab's limited support for some third-party integrations, which may require additional setup or workarounds. For teams that value data ownership and control, GitLab is a clear choice, while smaller teams or those already invested in the GitHub ecosystem may not need to switch.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setup
* Large enterprises that need self-hosting for compliance or security reasons
* Teams that require built-in CI/CD pipelines and are currently using third-party integrations on GitHub
* Developers who prioritize open-source software and want to support the MIT-licensed GitLab CE
* Teams with 10-50 users that don't require GitHub's proprietary features

## FAQ
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab free?
Yes, GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features than GitHub's free plan.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, GitLab provides an import tool that supports GitHub repositories.
### Does GitLab support third-party integrations?
Yes, but with limited support compared to GitHub.
### Is GitLab suitable for small teams?
Yes, but small teams may not require the additional features and complexity of GitLab.
